An injured employee is not required to accept work of a different or inferior kind merely because it pays the same amount. Once the alternative was classified as different or inferior, rejecting it was not an avoidable-loss failure. Other arguments Parker made about her original contractual rights were unnecessary to reach.

Ask which loss is claimed, how it follows from breach, what the defendant knew when agreeing, and whether the governing formulation also requires an undertaking of responsibility. Mere causal connection after the event is insufficient. Do not collapse this concept into foreseeability of reliance under promissory estoppel or foreseeability in tort; the time, purpose, and legal consequences differ. Foreseeability is objective: the Redgrave instruction asked what a reasonable person in the defendant's position knew or should have known when the contract was made, and the Cold Steel problem asks whether knowledge gained when a delivery date is later agreed counts. Under Article 2 buyers recover consequential damages but courts allow sellers only incidental ones (§§ 2-708(1), 2-710, 2-715), and courts have often held loss from a buyer's inability to cover foreseeable only if the seller knew facts making it so. Emotional-distress damages are excluded unless the breach also caused bodily harm or serious emotional disturbance was a particularly likely result (Restatement § 353); the more common approach allows them only for certain kinds of contract, such as funeral contracts (Lamm). A lost item's actual value to its owner is recoverable, but not unusual sentimental value (Mieske).

Identify the assumptions behind projections, the available market or operating evidence, causation, and the standard of review. The fact that a business is new is relevant to proof but should not be used as a substitute for examining the evidence under the applicable rule. Naval Institute supplies an earlier example of a supported counterfactual estimate. Courts divide on a lost chance: Collatz denied a quiz finalist recovery because winning could not be proved, while Chaplin v. Hicks valued the chance (Restatement § 348(3)). American courts have generally denied damages for lost reputation as uncertain or unforeseeable. Expert and statistical proof may establish royalties from a record already selling (Contemporary Mission), though not speculative follow-on tours, and the overwhelming majority of states allow proof of lost good will (AM/PM Franchise).

structuralAdditions (not registered: new.reason: Teaching gap: § 351(3) lets a court limit damages 'even for foreseeable loss' to avoid disproportionate compensation (C&M 1020 Note 3; Sundance Cruises); K-32 sent every foreseeable item straight to the certainty test, so Hadley with full notice and a £2 4s price had no such step.

new.label: Would full recovery of a foreseeable loss be disproportionate compensation?
new.detail: Even for a foreseeable loss, a court may exclude lost profits, allow only loss incurred in reliance, or otherwise limit damages if justice so requires to avoid disproportionate compensation (Restatement § 351(3)). Signs include an extreme disproportion between the loss and the price charged, informal dealing without a detailed written contract, and a non-commercial setting (§ 351 cmt. f, Illus. 17–19). Sundance Cruises held that an $85,000 classification fee could not have been intended to cover a $264 million claim.

Fera quotes Jarrait's rental-value measure for a lessor's failure to give possession (C&M 1036), and Coleman, J., says the plaintiffs 'are also entitled to the $1,000 deposit' (C&M 1039).
